A decorated Anglo-Saxon helmet of iron covered with stamped sheets of tinned bronze, found in 1939 in the ship-burial at Sutton Hoo, Suffolk. The visage carries eyebrows, a nose and a moustache which together with a dragon head form the image both of a human face and of a soaring winged dragon. Excavated as more than 500 rusted fragments accounting for less than half the original surface area, it was first reconstructed in 1945-46 and rebuilt in its present form in 1970-71.
Description E55: Type
The article records no maker, no place of manufacture and no date of manufacture. Everything asserted below about the making of the helmet is inference from the object and from comparanda, and is recorded as such.

cast bronze E57: Material

Held by five attachment points, its tang riveted to the cap beneath the neck of the upper dragon head. Two small round projecting plates on each side of the nose conceal rivets. An inlaid wire runs the length of the nasal ridge, beside which the background was punched down and filled with niello or another metallic inlay, leaving silvered triangles in relief; a tracer provided a grooved border on each side. Three punched circles per side run horizontally beside the nasal bridge, inlaid with silver. Below them run chased alternate rows of plain flutings and billeted strips, repeated vertically on the moustache; the bevelled lower lip repeats the circled pattern of the nasal bridge. Except where covered by the eyebrows and dragon head or inlaid with silver, the piece was heavily gilded.

a human face E1: CRM Entity The eyebrows, nose and moustache of the face mask create the image of a man.
winged dragon motif of the Sutton Hoo helmet E36: Visual Item
a dragon in flight E1: CRM Entity
A composite motif assembled from four separate fittings: the upper dragon head, the two eyebrows as wings, and the nose and moustache as body and tail. The dragon soars upwards and, at the dramatic focal point of the helmet, bares its teeth at the snake-like dragon flying down the crest. Because the eyebrows also terminate in boars' heads they may take a tertiary form as boars' bodies (Newton 1993, p. 37).
Design 1, dancing warriors E36: Visual Item
two men in civilian or ceremonial dress performing a spear or sword dance E1: CRM Entity
Known from six fragments and occurring four times on the helmet: on the two panels immediately above the eyebrows, and in the middle row of the dexter cheek guard on the panel closest to the face mask, with the symmetry of the helmet implying the same position on the opposite side. Their outer hands each hold two spears pointed towards their feet while their crossed hands grip swords; no single fragment shows both warriors, though the key fragment shows their crossed wrists. The full scene was inferred only after the first reconstruction, when Bruce-Mitford was shown the then unpublished Valsgaerde 7 helmet in Sweden. The dance has been associated with the cult of Odin.
Design 2, rider and fallen warrior E36: Visual Item
a mounted warrior trampling an enemy, with a small anthropomorphic figure kneeling on the horse's rump E1: CRM Entity
Known from eight fragments and representations. Thought to have appeared twelve times, on the assumption that Design 3 occupies a panel that originally held it. All panels appear to have been struck from the same die, so the horse and rider move clockwise around the helmet. The rider holds his spear overhead; the fallen man, grasping the reins in his left hand, thrusts a sword into the horse's chest with his right; the small figure clutches the spear together with the rider. Elements of victory and of defeat are combined and the symbolism is unclear; an overarching theme of fate has been proposed. Reconstruction relies in part on the Pliezhausen bracteate, which is complete and nearly identical though mirrored.
Design 3, unidentified figural scene E36: Visual Item
Known from seven small fragments, too small and ambiguous to allow the scene to be reconstructed; the article records no subject for it. Its presence is suggested between one and four times, and must have occurred towards the rear of the helmet on the dexter side. Fragment (a) shows parallel raised lines suggesting the body of a horse; fragment (b) shows two concentric raised lines two millimetres apart, apparently the rim of a shield of the same diameter as that held by the rider in Design 2. Bruce-Mitford proposed it as a variant rider scene used to repair a damaged Design 2 panel, but fragment (c) is out of context with the rest and he suggested it may have been a scrap placed under another piece to fill a gap.
Design 4, larger interlace E36: Visual Item
a single quadruped in ribbon style E1: CRM Entity
Occurs on the cheek guards, the neck guard and the skull cap, and was capable of complete reconstruction. Unlike the two identified figural scenes it appears in partial as well as full die impressions, and on the irregularly shaped cheek guards sometimes sideways. It has a billeted border on all sides; the animal's head sits in the upper centre of the panel, its eye defined by two circles, its jaws, neck, body and limbs formed of interlacing billeted and pellet-filled ribbons. Representative of what Salin termed Style II Germanic animal ornament.
Design 5, smaller interlace E36: Visual Item
two animals, upside down and reversed in relation to each other, with backward-turning heads E1: CRM Entity
Covered the face mask, was used prominently on the neck guard and filled several empty spaces on the cheek guards. Its die appears to have had a billeted border on only one each of its long and short sides, but on the neck guard the design shows borders along both long sides, suggesting the die was applied there as a continuous series of impressions on a large sheet of foil which was then cut.
the modification to the sinister eyebrow of the Sutton Hoo helmet E25: Human-Made Feature
The absence of hatched gold foil behind the garnets of the sinister eyebrow and behind the sinister eye of the upper dragon head. Seen in low light, with the garnets of only one brow reflecting, the helmet may have appeared to have a single eye. Whether this is deliberate or the trace of a repair is contested; see the attribute assignments below.
production of the Sutton Hoo helmet E12: Production
Neither the maker, the place nor the date of manufacture is recorded. The helmet is closer in character to the Swedish finds at Vendel and Valsgaerde than to any English parallel, and its class derives from the Roman infantry and cavalry helmets of the fourth- and fifth-century Constantinian workshops; a die stamp reported from Denmark has also been connected with it. Whether this indicates manufacture in Scandinavia or in England by a workshop in the Scandinavian tradition is not settled by the article.

time-span of the Sutton Hoo ship-burial E52: Time-Span 0613/0650 0620/0625 circa
One time-span, several opinions, following the instruction in the scope note of E61 Time Primitive that only one instance of E52 Time-Span should be created for a phenomenon and that multiple instances of E61 Time Primitive be attached to it to express multiple approximations. The commonly given estimate is circa 620-625 AD. The outer bound reflects the numismatic terminus post quem of 613-635 and Wilson's remark that the man buried may be any great man of East Anglia from 610 to 650. The superseded numismatic dating of 650-660 is recorded as an attribute assignment below rather than as a further time primitive here, because it was withdrawn rather than held alongside the present one.
The helmet was wrapped in cloths and placed to the left of the head of the body, among other regalia and instruments of power, in the chamber of a ship that had been hauled up from the nearby river and lowered into a prepared trench; an oval mound was then constructed around the ship.
collapse of the Sutton Hoo Mound 1 burial chamber S18: Alteration
Long after the burial the chamber roof collapsed violently under the weight of the mound, compressing the ship's contents into a seam of earth. The helmet is thought to have been shattered either by this collapse or by the force of another object falling on it; the article does not decide between them. Modelled as an instance of S18 Alteration, whose scope note covers natural events that permanently affect the form or consistency of a physical thing without changing its identity; CRMbase offers only the unspecific E5 Event for a non-intentional damage event.

Among its objectives were to survey the mound and its surroundings, to relocate the ship impression and excavate underneath, and to search the strata of the 1939 spoil dumps for fragments originally missed. As regards the helmet the excavation sought both positive and negative evidence: new crest fragments could go where Maryon had placed plaster, while their absence could be used to argue that the reconstructed crest was too long.
Four helmet fragments came from the second of the three 1939 dumps, which contained only items from the ship's burial chamber: a hinge piece from the dexter cheek guard, a surface flake from the crest, a small piece of iron with fluted lines, and a small piece of iron edging showing part of the larger interlace. The cheek guard piece joined a fragment found in 1939, together completing a hinge plate for one of the moving parts of the helmet. No substantial crest piece was found, which reinforced scepticism of the long plaster insertions in the first reconstruction.

the coroner's jury at the Sutton Hoo treasure trove inquest E74: Group Fourteen persons.
14 August 1939 E52: Time-Span 1939-08-14
Under the common law of treasure trove then in force, gold and silver that had been hidden and later rediscovered, the original owner being unknown, belonged to the crown; it was the hiding and not the abandoning that gave the king a property (Blackstone, Commentaries, 1765, p. 285). The jury found that the objects were not treasure trove and thus belonged to Pretty, the landowner, the dispositive point being that given the labour and publicity of dragging the ship up to the trench it was impossible to hold that the articles were buried or concealed secretly. The inquest is recorded as covering the fifty-six categories of remaining objects; the article states separately that items with only marginal amounts of gold or silver, such as the helmet, were not eligible for treasure trove in the first place and became the property of the landowner outright. Whether the helmet was among the objects actually before the inquest is therefore not clear from the article, and this assignment is recorded without resolving it.

possible ancient repair of a Design 2 panel of the Sutton Hoo helmet E11: Modification
Conjectural. Bruce-Mitford proposed that Design 3 is a variant rider scene used to replace a Design 2 panel damaged in antiquity, on the analogy of a unique pressblech design on the Valsgaerde 6 helmet, and pointed to the damage at the back of the helmet, where two centimetres of crest above the rear dragon head and most of that head itself are missing. Against it: the theory does not explain why the crest and rear dragon head were not themselves repaired, and fragment (c) is out of context with the rest of Design 3. Recorded here as an alteration whose occurrence is itself contested; the competing readings are given as attribute assignments below.

Maryon traced and detailed each fragment on stiff paper and segregated them by decoration, markings and thickness; adjoining pieces were adhered with Durofix and held in a box of sand while the adhesive hardened. The pieces were then set on a human-sized plaster head he sculpted, with added layers to account for the original lining. Skull cap fragments were stuck on with Plasticine or set into spaces cut into the head, then fixed permanently with strong white plaster which, mixed with brown umber, also filled the gaps; the cheek guards, neck guard and visor were placed onto shaped, plaster-covered wire mesh and joined to the cap.
Criticised, though at the time almost entirely not in print, for arranging the fragments around the mould of an average man's head and so possibly predetermining the size; for the exposed jaw left by the missing front of each cheek piece, the hole between eyebrows and nose, and eye holes large enough for a sword to pass through; for a fixed rather than movable neck guard; for a projecting face mask that would have left the nose vulnerable; and for the use of plaster to elongate the crest by approximately four and a half inches.

the 1945-46 restoration fill of the Sutton Hoo helmet E22: Human-Made Object
plaster E57: Material
wire mesh E57: Material
The cheek guards, face mask and neck guard were removed and x-rayed, revealing the wire mesh covered in plaster and overlaid by fragments. The wire was rolled back like a carpet and a saw used to separate each fragment; the remaining plaster was chipped away with a scalpel and needles. The skull cap was cut in half by pushing off the crest with long pins inserted through the bottom of the plaster head and slicing through the middle; the central plaster core was removed and the remaining thin skin of plaster and iron separated into individual fragments. The process left the helmet in more than 500 fragments. Some damage occurred: part of the fragment of Design 1 showing the face and body of a dancing warrior was crushed, and its nose and mouth were later restored.
Modelled as E80 Part Removal, and the removed material as a part, rather than as an E81 Transformation. The scope note of E80 directs total decomposition of an object into pieces to E81, but the scope note of E24 states that interventions of conservation and repair are not regarded to produce a new human-made thing. What was removed was the modern fill added in 1945-46; the ancient fragments were separated but remained the helmet, which kept its registration number throughout. See the notes file.

New joins were found mostly by looking at the backs of the fragments, whose blackened, rippled surfaces could be matched under a microscope. The skull cap was built out from the crest, aided by the discovery that only the two fluted strips bordering the crest were gilded. The cheek guards were shaped and substantially lengthened by joining three fragments from the sinister side of the first reconstruction with two from the dexter side; the exposed areas by the jaw were eliminated only near the end, when an expert on arms and armour advised that the cheek guards should simply switch sides. The repositioned fragments were placed against a featureless plaster dome built outwards with oil-free plasticine to match the original dimensions, held with long pins while jute and adhesive were moulded to the missing areas; the fragment edges were coated with water-resistant resin and plaster was spread over the jute, then painted light brown with the panel edges drawn in.
Differences from the first reconstruction: a third row on the cheek guards, a Design 4 panel in the middle row replaced by Design 1, and the cheek guards switched sides. The visor and neck guard carry the same designs in both.
Known errors, all in the neck guard, where very little original substance survives that can be positioned with any certainty: several Design 5 fragments are placed too high, leaving more space below the transverse fluted strips than above, whereas the configuration should allow two full impressions of Design 5 of equal length joined vertically; seven vertical strips of Design 5 are shown though there is no evidence for that number and five is equally possible; the two strips flanking the central one show an implausible inward tilt; and the neck guard hangs lower than it would have when made, since its top originally fitted inside the cap, leaving the abutting edges of the dexter cheek and neck guards at different levels. Two blocks of fragments on the bottom edge and four in the middle are only speculatively placed.

Raedwald of East Anglia E21: Person
King of the East Angles, of the Wuffingas dynasty, whose seat is believed to have been at Rendlesham, four and a quarter miles upriver from Sutton Hoo. Almost all that is recorded of him comes from Bede. His death can be conservatively dated between 616 and 633 on Bede alone.
The preferred candidate, but by no means conclusive. The case rests on the dating of the burial, the abundance of wealth and of items identified as regalia, and, befitting a king who kept two altars, the presence of both Christian and pagan influences. The helmet contributes to it: it displays both wealth and power, and the modification to the sinister eyebrow has been read as linking the wearer to the one-eyed Odin.

The rival reading, recorded here as an assignment that declines to assign. The desire to link a burial with a known and famous name outstrips the evidence; the burial is certainly a commemorative display of wealth and power but does not necessarily memorialise Raedwald, or a king, and could theoretically have been a votive offering (Carver 1986, p. 83). The case for Raedwald depends heavily on the coins, whose dating is precise only within two decades and whose chronologies have shifted before. Wilson: the little word "may" should be brought into any identification of Raedwald; it may be Sigeberht, or his illegitimate brother, or any other great man of East Anglia from 610 to 650.

Current. Thirty-seven gold Merovingian coins, three blanks and two small ingots were found in a purse and offer the most objective means of dating the burial. Later studies took the specific gravity of some 700 Merovingian gold coins, which were minted with predictably decreasing purity over time, to estimate a coin's date from the fineness of its gold; this suggests the latest coins in the purse were minted between 613 and 635 AD and most likely closer to the beginning of that range. The range is a tentative terminus post quem only: sometime later, perhaps after a period of years, the coins were collected and buried. Generally consistent with, but not exclusive to, Raedwald.

The two brows may have been manufactured in different ways while being intended to look essentially the same. That the absence of foils results from a repair, and presumably a shortage of gold, seems unlikely given the minute quantities needed; and given the skill required to shape the gold cell walls and cut the garnets so precisely, the omission on the left brow appears deliberate. The repair theory also does not account for the absence of gold foil behind one of the garnet dragon eyes. Seen in low light, with only one brow's garnets reflecting, the helmet may have seemed to have a single eye, linking its wearer to the one-eyed god.
